tldr: Inspired by the brain's cerebral hemispheres and the corpus callosum, researchers developed a two-arm musculoskeletal controller made of two recurrent modules connected by a delayed communication channel. Under signal-dependent noise and energetic constraints, it dramatically outperforms a single large monolithic model in robustness. The results show that inter-module communication reshapes control strategies by improving endpoint accuracy, saving energy, and suppressing muscle co-contraction.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of the proposed bilateral modular controller. Two GRU modules receive shared sensory inputs and exchange internal states via a delayed linear communication channel, outputting activation commands for 12 muscles under signal-dependent noise and energetic constraints.
overview:
To move musculoskeletal robots smoothly and accurately in the real world, controllers must handle energetic constraints and signal-dependent noise, where actuator variance scales with command magnitude. However, when a single large network (a monolithic architecture) tries to meet the competing demands of trajectory following and postural stabilization against disturbances, it struggles under noise and resource constraints.

To address this, the authors took inspiration from the mammalian brain, which is divided into left and right hemispheres that coordinate via the corpus callosum despite neural conduction delays. They designed a "bilateral modular controller" by splitting the controller into two GRU modules connected by a learnable communication channel with delay. This architecture was trained end-to-end in the "MotorNet" differentiable musculoskeletal simulator on interleaved reaching and holding tasks.

The experiments revealed that simply adopting a modular structure dramatically boosts task success rates and disturbance robustness compared to a capacity-matched monolithic model. Furthermore, introducing delayed communication between modules does more than just boost performance: it reshapes the "quality" of the control strategy in favorable ways, reducing wasteful simultaneous muscle contraction (co-contraction) and achieving higher endpoint precision at lower energetic costs.
contributions: Proposed a two-module musculoskeletal controller inspired by the brain's bilateral hemispheric organization, linked by a communication channel with delay
Demonstrated that modular controllers substantially outperform capacity-matched monolithic controllers under signal-dependent noise and energetic constraints
Discovered that inter-module communication under non-zero delay reshapes control strategy trade-offs, suppressing muscle co-contraction and saving energy
Captured emerging signs of lateralization, where inter-module communication increases output contributions to the contralateral arm despite starting from a symmetric architecture

sections.heading: Why split controllers into modules like the brain?
sections.summary: Real-world musculoskeletal control requires balancing precision and stability while accounting for signal-dependent noise and energy constraints. Inspired by bilateral motor control in the brain, this work aims to test the benefits of modularization itself and examine how delayed communication shapes control strategies.
sections.details:
When operating robots in the real world, noise-free environments do not exist. In biological systems, muscles suffer from "signal-dependent noise," where motor command variance scales with command magnitude. Reaching accurately and maintaining posture against disturbances under noise and energetic limits is an exceptionally difficult challenge.

Looking at the mammalian motor system, the brain is divided into left and right cerebral hemispheres that communicate through a dense bundle of nerve fibers called the "corpus callosum." Interestingly, even though this communication channel suffers from physical conduction delays, the two hemispheres divide roles complementarily to achieve dexterous motor control.

Aiming toward controlling complex bodies like humanoid robots, this study poses two core questions: First, does splitting into a modular architecture itself improve performance under realistic constraints? Second, how does inter-module communication reshape the resulting control strategy? The authors answer these questions through rigorous comparisons against monolithic models in a differentiable simulator.

sections.heading: From biological lateralization to modular robot control
sections.summary: This section reviews neuroscience studies on handedness and bimanual coordination alongside computational motor control models. Prior work on modular control and lateralization has largely focused on language and vision, leaving the role of communication under strict physical constraints in musculoskeletal control largely unexplored.
sections.details:
In motor neuroscience, researchers have long studied how the left and right hemispheres play distinct roles in trajectory control and postural stabilization, constantly interacting with each other. Computational approaches have similarly framed motor behavior as an optimization problem over biomechanics, forward predictions, and sensory feedback.

Meanwhile, robotics and machine learning have explored modular control via reinforcement learning and Mixture-of-Experts architectures. However, most prior studies focused primarily on task scores or representation learning. Almost none isolated and evaluated the distinct effects of "structural modularity" versus "inter-module communication" under matched biomechanical constraints and actuator noise.

Taking inspiration from bio-inspired structures, this work bridges the gap by conducting systematic ablations on the presence of communication channels and transmission delays.

sections.heading: Designing the differentiable musculoskeletal environment and bilateral controller
sections.summary: The authors built an environment with two planar 2-DOF arms (12 muscles) in MotorNet and designed the proposed model using two GRUs alongside baseline models. Training incorporates signal-dependent noise, energy loss, and ring-buffer-based discrete communication delays across interleaved reach-and-hold tasks.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Musculoskeletal Simulation Environment
The experiments use the differentiable musculoskeletal simulator "MotorNet." Each arm has planar 2 degrees of freedom, driven by 6 Hill-type muscle models spanning the shoulder and elbow, yielding 12 muscles across both arms (Figure F1 A).

### 3.2 Controller Architecture
The main proposed model, "Bilateral w/ CC," places two GRU modules with hidden size 64 on each side, linked by a communication channel with delay $\delta$. A linear combination of the bilateral hidden states outputs 12-dimensional muscle activation commands. For baselines, the authors prepared "Bilateral w/o CC" (severed communication line) and a capacity-matched single GRU (hidden size 128) called "Monolithic."

### 3.3 Realistic Physical Constraints
Three biologically plausible constraints were applied:
- Signal-dependent noise: Multiplicative Gaussian noise proportional to the command magnitude is injected into muscle commands.
- Energetic cost: A penalty weight $\lambda_{\mathrm{energy}}$ scales the sum of squared muscle commands to curb wasteful high-amplitude actions.
- Communication delay: Past hidden states from the counterpart module are held in a ring buffer and received via linear projection after a discrete step delay $\delta$.

### 3.4 Evaluation Tasks
The controller is trained and evaluated on interleaved tasks: a "Reach" task targeting 8 radial directions and a "Hold" task maintaining endpoint position against unknown disturbances (Gaussian force with 0.5 N standard deviation) (Figure F1 B, C).

captions.F1: Musculoskeletal model and task design used in this work. (A) Planar arm with 6 muscles consisting of mono- and bi-articular muscles at the shoulder and elbow. (B) 8-direction reaching task. (C) Postural holding task resisting disturbance forces to maintain the target position.

sections.heading: Modular architectures deliver immense robustness while communication reshapes strategy
sections.summary: Under noise and energy constraints, modular controllers maintained substantially higher success rates than the monolithic baseline. Furthermore, delayed inter-module communication improved endpoint precision, cut energetic costs, and lowered muscle co-contraction, alongside emerging contralateral lateralization patterns.
sections.details:
### 4.2 Modularity is the Primary Driver of Robustness
Across a grid of noise coefficients $k$ and energy penalties $\lambda$, the proposed model and the communication-free modular model dramatically outperformed the Monolithic baseline (Figure F3 A). In intermediate noise regimes ($k=0.05, 0.1$), the monolithic success rate plummeted to 38.00%–53.00%, whereas modular architectures maintained consistently high success rates (Figure F3 B).

### 4.3 Decomposition of Kinematic and Muscle Metrics
According to the metric breakdown in Table 1, models with delayed communication ($d>0$) achieved top scores across all metrics: success rate, endpoint error, trajectory error, postural variance, energetic cost, and co-contraction index (CCI). While the non-communicating model (Bilateral w/o CC) achieved decent task success, it fell behind the delayed-communication model in endpoint accuracy and muscle co-contraction.

### 4.4 Communication Reshapes Control Strategies
The true value of communication shows up in *how* tasks are accomplished. As shown in Figure F4, delayed communication models significantly reduced muscle co-contraction (the strategy of stiffening joints by co-activating antagonist muscles), trimming unnecessary muscle output to save energy. In generalization tests under unencountered conditions—a wider reach radius (0.16 m) and stronger disturbances (2.0 N)—the delayed communication model also achieved the highest success rate (Figure F5).

### 4.5 Emergence of Lateralization
Analyzing trained weights revealed that models with a communication channel had a higher Contralateral Index (CI), allocating stronger outputs to contralateral arm muscles (0.0177 vs. 0.0001 without communication). A virtual lesion experiment (inactivating one module) showed a matching impact pattern, suggesting that communication naturally fosters a functional division of labor across sides.

captions.F3: Comparison profile of task success rates. (A) Distribution of success rates across all experimental configurations. Modular models substantially outperform the monolithic model. (B) Grid map across noise and energy constraints. While the monolithic baseline (Mono.) collapses in intermediate noise regimes, modular models remain exceptionally stable.
captions.F4: Breakdown of energetic cost, co-contraction index (CCI), and success rate across constraints. In low-to-medium noise regimes, models with delayed communication (green) achieve a superior trade-off, sustaining high success rates while curbing co-contraction and energy consumption.
captions.F5: Generalization performance under unseen, harsher conditions. The delayed communication model (Bi w/ CC d>0) maintained the highest success rate in both "Reach-16" (farther targets) and "Hold-2N" (quadrupled disturbance force).

sections.heading: Design principles for robot control inspired by the brain
sections.summary: The authors conclude that modularity lays the foundation for robustness, while delayed communication tunes multi-objective trade-offs. They discuss simulation limitations and future directions toward applications in humanoid robotics.
sections.details:
### Conclusions and Insights
The key takeaway from this work is that "more communication is not always better." Simply partitioning a controller into two modules establishes a resilient baseline for tasks where noise and energetic constraints interact. Inter-module communication does not merely boost performance; it reconfigures the operational regime, tuning how the system balances precision, stability, actuation cost, and joint stiffness.

Furthermore, the finding that contralateral control structures emerge naturally through communication—despite starting from symmetric modules—offers intriguing insights into the computational origins of functional lateralization in the brain.

### Limitations and Future Work
However, this model is an engineering abstraction using supervised loss and simple delayed linear channels, rather than a literal replica of biological brains. Tasks were also limited to reaching and holding individual arms, without complex bimanual coordination. Future work will need to increase task complexity and examine communication bottlenecks when scaling to physical humanoid hardware.

sections.heading: Appendix: Uncovering the monolithic model's "apparent success" under high noise
sections.summary: This diagnostic examines why the monolithic model showed a sudden V-shaped recovery in success rates under extreme noise. It reveals a "fake stability" trap where the model avoided noise by shutting down muscle activity, a strategy that completely collapses under stronger disturbances.
sections.details:
During the main experiments, the monolithic model exhibited a curious V-shaped recovery in success rate under the highest noise condition ($k=0.2$). Why did this happen?

The answer lies in the nature of signal-dependent noise. If muscle commands are kept near zero, injected noise and energetic cost also drop to near zero. Because the training disturbances (0.5 N standard deviation) were relatively gentle, a passive "slack strategy"—going limp and doing nothing—could accidentally satisfy the hold threshold.

To test this hypothesis, the authors evaluated performance under disturbance standard deviations of 1.5 N and 4.0 N (Figure F7). While success held up under moderate forces, it suffered a catastrophic collapse to floor levels (nearly 0%) under 4.0 N disturbances. This proves that the monolithic model never learned active resistance; it merely went limp to avoid noise. This highlights the vital importance of inspecting internal actuator states and muscle outputs during evaluation.

captions.F7: Diagnostic of apparent success rates under varying disturbance magnitudes. When the disturbance standard deviation is increased to 4.0 N (right panel), the monolithic model's apparent success under high noise (k=0.2) completely collapses, proving it failed to learn active control.

takeaways: In robotic control facing actuator noise and energy constraints, modular architectures are far more resilient and robust than capacity-matched monolithic models.
Inter-module communication acts as a tuning knob for control strategies, reducing wasteful muscle co-contraction and trimming energy use rather than simply altering binary task success.
Communication delays (latency) do not necessarily break control; systems can learn effective, specialized control regimes specifically under non-zero delay.
When training under signal-dependent noise, models can easily fall into a "slack trap" of turning off commands to bypass noise, making rigorous disturbance diagnostics essential.
limitations: Experiments are restricted to planar 2-DOF arms in the MotorNet simulator, leaving real-world robotic dynamics like physical friction unverified.
The benchmarks do not involve true bimanual coordination tasks, such as both arms collaboratively manipulating a single object.
The communication channel uses a simple delayed linear projection, which does not capture biological neural spiking or advanced information compression protocols.
